title: A nonidentity bijection
prompt: Give a bijection N->N that is not the identity. Use N={0,1,2,...}.

solution.text: Define f(0)=1, f(1)=0, and f(n)=n for n>=2.
The values 0 and 1 are swapped and every other value is fixed. Thus each output has exactly one preimage.
Hence f is injective and surjective, and f(0)!=0 so it is not the identity.

title: Neither injective nor onto

The number 1 has no preimage, so the function is not onto.

title: Composition injection trap
prompt: Disprove: if f composed with g is one-to-one, then f is one-to-one.

solution.text: Let g:{0}->{0,1} send 0 to 0. Let f:{0,1}->{0} send both inputs to 0.
The composition f o g has a singleton domain, so it is injective.
But f(0)=f(1) with 0!=1, so f is not injective.

subject: dm
title: Countability of integers

solution.text: List the integers as 0,1,-1,2,-2,3,-3,... .
Every integer occurs once: 0 first, each positive k at index 2*k-1, and -k at index 2*k.
This gives a bijection from N={0,1,...} to Z, so Z is countably infinite.

title: Uncountable sets with countable difference
prompt: Give uncountable A,B for which A-B is countably infinite.

solution.text: Take A=R and B=R-Z.
B is uncountable: otherwise R=B union Z would be a union of two countable sets and thus countable.
A-B=Z, which is countably infinite. Both required sets are uncountable.

subject: dm
title: Uncountability diagonal argument
prompt: Explain why the set of infinite binary sequences is uncountable.

solution.text: Assume a list s1,s2,... contains every infinite binary sequence.
Define t by choosing its nth bit different from the nth bit of sn.
Then t differs from sn in position n for each n, so t is missing from the list.
This contradiction shows no countable list exists. The set is uncountable.

subject: dm
title: Countability trap
prompt: Explain why infinite binary sequences are uncountable while finite binary strings and the rational numbers are countable.

solution.text: Finite binary strings can be listed by length, then lexicographically; rationals have a countable diagonal listing.
For any proposed list of infinite binary sequences, flip the nth bit of the nth sequence.
The resulting sequence is absent from the list, proving uncountability.

title: Both differences countably infinite
prompt: Find uncountable A,B such that A-B and B-A are both countably infinite.

solution.text: Let I=R-Z, E={2*k:k in Z}, O={2*k+1:k in Z}. Define A=I union E and B=I union O.
I is uncountable, so A and B are uncountable. E and O are disjoint.
A-B=E and B-A=O, both countably infinite.
